prompt: A cyclist's velocity (m/s) is recorded every $2$ seconds: at $t = 0, 2, 4, 6$ the readings are $5, 8, 10, 7$. Use a right Riemann sum with $3$ subintervals to estimate the distance traveled, in meters, from $t = 0$ to $t = 6$.
hint: Distance is the area under the velocity graph. Each subinterval is $2$ seconds wide; a RIGHT sum uses the reading at the END of each subinterval.

hints.text: Distance is the area under the velocity graph. Each subinterval is $2$ seconds wide; a RIGHT sum uses the reading at the END of each subinterval.
Right endpoints are $t = 2, 4, 6$ with velocities $8, 10, 7$. Multiply each by $2$ seconds.

explanation: Estimated distance $= 2 \cdot 8 + 2 \cdot 10 + 2 \cdot 7 = 50$ m. (The left sum would give $2(5 + 8 + 10) = 46$ m; the truth is somewhere around there.)

alternativeExplanations.title: Units make it concrete
steps: Velocity (m/s) times time (s) gives meters. Each term is a distance for one $2$-second stretch.
Pretending the cyclist held $8$ m/s for the first $2$ s, $10$ m/s for the next $2$ s and $7$ m/s for the last $2$ s gives $16 + 20 + 14 = 50$ m.
That is exactly what a right Riemann sum assumes.
